title: The Assistant Must Not Become the Store
description: I am connecting an assistant to the catalog so it can ask. If I pour the files into the model instead, the catalog was for nothing.
body:
I am connecting an assistant to VALESKA. The deficit in front of me is that the useful-looking way to do it destroys the store. Pour the repository into the model and hope the model remembers. That is convenient for a demonstration. When the conversation ends, the permissions never made the trip, and what you have left is a plausible summary with no record to inspect. The assistant has become the filing cabinet. I need the opposite: an assistant that can ask an index which remains when the conversation is gone.

So I am not putting the files in the chat. The files, the classifications, and the embeddings have to live where they can be reviewed tomorrow by someone who was not in the conversation. A librarian does not become the library because she can walk the stacks. She uses a catalog that remains when she leaves. The assistant should be able to request a scan, ask a question in ordinary language, and read what the tools return. It should not replace those returns with an opaque history. When she leaves, the shelves are still there.

A client of the catalog

The work today is a client, not a second memory. Five tools already sit on the index — search, classify, scan, list categories, retrieve file information. The client speaks to that server and maps the assistant’s requests onto those tools. Context is carried between the two so a question can follow a scan, but the record stays in the platform. The code is written so a provider can be swapped: an abstract interface, a Claude implementation, a runner that executes a playbook. That is an interface. It is not a claim that several vendors are in daily use. The tests construct the client with a fake key. They do not prove a live model call. They prove the assistant is wired to the catalog, not standing in for it.

Two playbooks turn that wiring into a method another person can repeat. One onboards a codebase: scan a directory, then ask what languages, components, and shape the project has. The other investigates a feature: take a question in ordinary language, turn it into semantic search, and return material about a function. Both are the same sequence the catalog already implies — establish the scope, gather evidence, interpret the return, propose a next look. They are prompt-shaped methods on top of the tools. They are not a recorded run against a stranger’s tree, and they are not a place to keep the tree. If the playbook’s answer cannot be checked against the index, it is a chat again.

Seeing disorder is not permission to rearrange it

The same commit lays a chaos-recovery agent. The intent is the same deficit, pointed at disorder in a tree: notice deep nesting, mixed types, and poor names; draft an organization plan; estimate risk; let a person confirm before anything moves. The execution path is supposed to include safety checks and a dry run. The file is a foundation. Several of its scores are still placeholders. A system that can see disorder should be able to explain the evidence and propose a sequence. It should not confuse that proposal with authority to rearrange the project. Moving files without confirmation would be the migration I am not running.

Four tests pass: client initialization, tool communication, playbook execution, and end-to-end integration. Read them as construction tests. They do not stand in for a live session or a live assistant. What they do establish is the result I needed today: an assistant can be pointed at the catalog instead of being asked to become the filing cabinet. The open work is to run those playbooks against a codebase we did not write, and to make recovery something a person can confirm rather than a skeleton. Until then I have a client I can execute, not a claim that the assistant already understands the work.

Historical basis: VALESKA Phase 3 commit 8a5aa55, November 30, 2025; contemporaneous Phase 3 summary, valeska/ai_client.py, valeska/chaos_recovery_agent.py, and test_phase3.py. The Phase 3 summary is internally dated December 2025; the commit timestamp is the publication-date authority.
